title: [BUG] `@auth` doesn't attach OpenAPI `security` requirement, docs UI never sends the key
description:
## Description

When you protect an endpoint with `#* @auth <guard_name>`, the API access works correctly, but the Try It Out or Authorise in the docs, no matter what flavour you use, fails. The key is never sent, and every endpoint sends a `400 Bad Request`, causing confusion.

## To Reproduce

1. Create a plumber2 API with an `@authGuard` and an endpoint tagged `@auth <guard_name>`
2. Start the API and open the docs page (e.g. `/__docs__/`)
3. Click "Authorise", enter a valid key
4. Click "Try it out" on the protected endpoint
5. Request fails with 400

Another way to check this is to check `openapi.json` directly: `components.securitySchemes` has the guard listed correctly, but the operation itself (e.g. `paths./health.get`) has no `security` field at all.

## Expected Behaviour

The protected endpoint's OpenAPI operation should include a `security` requirement referencing the guard, so docs UIs know to attach the key automatically.

title: inconsistent "Argument" documentation
description:
In the annotations page, the "@body" tag (among a few) suggests it can be `Name[:Type][(Default)][*][Description]`. In my experience, that means that:

- `Name` is required
- if you want a `Type`, it must be preceded by a colon
- if you want a `Default` value, it must be enclosed in parens
- if you want it to be required, add `*` after all of name, type, default (some optional) and before an optional description
- if you want a `Description`, it must be enclosed in brackets

However, the verbiage states

> _If a single @body tag is used the Name can be omitted to indicate that the body is not a named object but simply an instance of the given Type_

Ignoring the "name is required" part, it then makes sense that in this case I should do `#* @body :string`, but that fails with

```
Caused by error in `type_caster(content$schema, isTRUE(desc$required), loc = "body")`:
! argument "name" is missing, with no default
```

What works is `#* @body string`, but that could mean Name="string" or Type="string".

I suggest `plumber2` supports the format directed by the "Argument" string that says the type needs to be preceded by the Name. Whether or not you impose stricter parsing is a discussion for backward compatibility.

---

But even with that, `@body`, `@body quux:quux`, `@body quux`, and `@body binary` all make no difference to me, the `function(body)` still works as one might think. For this, Is my `@parser raw` impacting things?

```r
plumber2::register_parser(
  name       = "raw",
  fun        = function() function(raw, directives) raw,
  mime_types = "*/*",
  default    = FALSE
)
```

(Do you think adding a native parser that always always always returns "raw binary" regardless of what is claimed? "octet" fails when the caller specifies a content-type, I want to ignore what the caller claims.

title: Memory duplication when scaling ML models – any plan to support shared memory / copy‑on‑write?
description:
First, thank you for plumber2 – it's a fantastic tool.

When scaling an API that serves a large ML model, each worker process loads its own full copy of the model. On Linux, a forking model (like RestRserve + Rserve) would allow copy‑on‑write sharing, drastically reducing memory usage and cloud costs.

I understand plumber2 is built on httpuv/libuv, which isn't fork‑safe. But is there any interest in:

- an optional fork‑based backend (even experimental)?
- helpers to load models into shared memory (e.g., via `mmap`)?
- official guidance to delegate prediction to a separate forking service?

If not, I'll continue using workarounds. Just wanted to raise this as a real pain point for production ML in R.

Thanks again.

title: `array_caster()` stack overflow when `@body` item is array of objects
description:
Hi there,

Ran into an issue when building a post endpoint, which had an `@body` annotation for an array of objects (`items:[{name:string, email:string}]`) which caused a stack overflow at request time when the handler's `body` param is first evaluated. Removing this typing from the `@body` annotation allows it to run as expected.

I, with some AI assistance, believe the issue is in `array_caster()` in `R/type_caster.R` - the var `caster` is being reassigned to a function in the if/else statement, so at request time the enclosing environment of `caster()` is different than when it was created.

reprex (passing `{"items": [{"name": "foo", "email": "foo@bar.com"}]}` as body in post request):
```
library(plumber2)

api() |>
  api_logger(
    logger = logger_console(),
    access_log_format = combined_log_format
  ) |>
  api_post(
    path = "/test",
    handler = function(body) { body },
    parsers = get_parsers("json"),
    doc = openapi_operation(
      request_body = openapi_request_body(
        content = openapi_content(
          "application/json" = openapi_schema(
            x = I("object"),
            properties = list(
              items = list(
                type = "array",
                items = list(
                  type = "object",
                  properties = list(
                    name = list(type = "string"),
                    email = list(type = "string")
                  )
                )

            )
          )
        )

  api = test_api,

)
```

title: Conditional GETs
description:
It would be neat if plumber2 supported conditional GETs out of the box. I suspect I could use the  tag creation functionality to do it myself, but it would be a nice to have for improving server-side rendered HTML applications.

Using an etag, plumber2 could automatic respond with a 304 Not Modified and short-circuit the response if the client's If-None-Match matches the server. This would speed up server responses and reduce repetitive computations. Perhaps the etag generation mechanism could be specified by a roxygen tag too.

Eg

```r
#' @get /
#' @etag Sys.Date()
function() {
   my_html()
}
```

In this example, on a 200 OK, the server would return the normal response body as well as etag generated via Sys.Date(). Subsequent gets from the same client would return a 304 to the client if the client's etag date matches the server's (via string equality).

**Scope**: only applies to GET/HEAD routes, & no response body is sent

**References**
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Conditional_requests
- https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionController/ConditionalGet.html


> As an aside (and probably out of scope for this issue), being able to have a @cache tag to automatically cache responses would be nice. We can do this manually atm via eg memoise and client id, but it would make these patterns more discoverable and feel more "batteries included" particularly for SSR purposes

title: Is it possible to "pass through" mime type?

```r
    function() {},
    route = "my_route"
  )
```


Then the mime type and serialisation of all routes before it is lost, even if the route doesn't modify anything. Is it possible to retain the mime type or serialisation of the response body when using middleware like this?

JSON (de)serialization performance
description: Given that there is a real effort for a rethinking of plumber in this package, I would love for this team to consider ways to improve the performance of json serialization and deserialization. While `jsonlite` is a tried and true method for parsing and serializing json, the R community has created far more performant alternatives. Most notably, I believe these are `yyjsonr`, `RcppSimdJson`, and `jsonify`. Below I compare the use of yyjsonr as an alternative to jsonlite in the existing {plumber} package as motivation. ## Serialization For smaller data, jsonlite is a very solid performer. However, as the size of the object that we need to serialize grows, its performance gets outshined. Below is a the output of `bench::press()` where the penguins dataset (shouts out R 4.5) is sampled 10, 100, 10_000, 100_000, and 1_000_000, times. Each sample is done 25 times. conn <- DBI::dbConnect(...)

title: Performance testing
description:
We might as well iron out obvious performance issues before we release. plumber2 obviously adds overhead to  fiery (+routr) be the mere act of making it easier to set up more complex apis. Without falling into the trap of premature optimisation, the following areas are where I might expect improvements to be found:

* `routr::Route$dispatch()` as it sequentially tests the regex related to each path. The paths has been sorted by priority, so it exits as soon as possible, but I would be happy if we could avoid the r-side loop. In general it would be interesting if we could add support for precompilation of regexes in stringi so we could do all that up front and avoid the overhead of compiling them at every request (unless stringi already caches regexes)
* Content negotiation in reqres could potentially be improved
* `Request` object construction in reqres. I honestly don't think it can be done much faster since almost all parsing is delayed until the user request it

I'm sure I'm missing something obvious. It might also be that it is already as low-overhead as possible because past-me was more clever than I give credit for

title: Support promises
description:
This is the only remaining plumber feature to add and is of course important.

It will require coordinated updates in plumber2, fiery, and routr

- [ ] In routr, `RouteStack$dispatch()` needs to understand promises as return values and construct the remaining execution of the stack accordingly
- [ ] In fiery, `Fire$p_trigger()` needs to be able to do the same. Further, `Fire$request_logic()` needs to be able to wrap up correctly if a promise is returned
- [ ] In plumber2, `create_plumber_request_handler()` needs to be able to handle a promise returned from a handler and wrap up correctly. Special care needs to be taken for graphics serializers, though I'm not sure the complexity present in plumber is needed (bracing myself to be proven wrong)
